ORDER INSTITUTING PROCEEDING UNDER SECTION 206 OF THE FEDERAL 
POWER ACT AND CONSOLIDATING WITH OTHER PROCEEDINGS 
 
COMMENTS OF CLEAN AIR TASK FORCE 
 
Pursuant to Rule 211 of the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission’s (“Commission”) 
Rules of Practice and Procedure, 18 C.F.R. § 385.211, Clean Air Task Force, Inc. 
(“CATF”) respectfully submits these comments responding to the filings of the parties in the 
Show Cause Order pursuant to section 206 of the Federal Power Act (“FPA”) dated February 20, 
2025, seeking information about whether the Open Access Transmission Tariff (“OATT”) of 
PJM Interconnection, L.L.C. (“PJM”), “remains just and reasonable and not unduly 
discriminatory or preferential without provisions addressing with sufficient clarity or consistency 
the rates, terms, and conditions of service that apply to co-location arrangements; or (2)

3 
 
 
explain[ing] what changes to the Tariff would [be necessary to] remedy the identified 
concerns.”1 
CATF is a nonprofit organization dedicated to advancing the policy and technology 
changes necessary to achieve a zero-emissions high-energy planet at an affordable cost. With 
more than 25 years of internationally recognized expertise on environmental policy and law, and 
a commitment to exploring all potential solutions, CATF is a pragmatic, non-ideological 
advocacy group with the bold ideas needed to address climate change and air pollution. CATF 
has offices in Boston, Washington, D.C., and Brussels, with staff working remotely around the 
world.   
CATF thanks the Commission for initiating this inquiry. CATF’s interest in this docket 
arises from our mission, which includes working towards a transition to a clean and sustainable 
energy system, where costs are just and reasonable for all. Such a future requires careful 
planning for the transmission development and services required to support the addition of new 
loads and new generation. The recent and imminent surge in demand for co-located generation to 
serve data centers and other large loads makes holistic grid planning even more critical to 
ensuring that transmission rates, practices, and procedures are just, reasonable, and not unduly 
discriminatory. It is CATF’s view that, not just in PJM, FERC must consider the issues presented 
here as it engages with transmission planners across the country on regional planning, going 
beyond a case-by-case approach to create generally applicable rules for integrating new large 
loads onto the grid, with or without co-located generation. Furthermore, until such generally 
applicable rules are created, FERC should not approve any waivers for interconnection service 
agreements.  
 
1 PJM Interconnection, L.L.C., Order Instituting Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act and 
Consolidating with Other Proceedings at ¶ 2, Docket Nos. EL25-49-000, et al. (“Show Cause Order”).

4 
 
 
As an initial matter, CATF supports the comments made by Public Interest Organizations 
(PIOs)2 and the Union of Concerned Scientists3 in this docket, and submits this additional letter 
to provide a few supplemental points of specific concern to CATF. 
I. CO-LOCATED GENERATION TO SERVE LARGE LOADS CANNOT BE 
FULLY ISOLATED FROM THE GRID 
As an initial matter, CATF bases its position on the physical reality that existing and new 
generation that is designated to serve large loads cannot be isolated from the rest of the 
transmission system. CATF supports the conclusions of PJM, Indicated PJM Transmission 
Owners, Public Service Gas & Electric, and the Union of Concerned Scientists that all co-located 
load is Network Load, cannot be fully isolated, and inevitably uses and also impacts the 
transmission system.4 The co-located load, co-located generator, and transmission system are not 
only physically connected, but inter-reliant. As such, while fully isolated load configurations 
may be spelled out in contractual arrangements, the claim that they do not take necessary 
services from the transmission system is simply not factually supported by the physical operation 
of the system. Co-located operations routinely include unplanned generator run-backs or 
reductions in output, generator MW output oscillations, and co-located load utilization 
fluctuations. When these conditions occur, they result in “brief, but routine, imbalances between 
the load and the generation that would need to rely on the grid to balance.”5  
 
2 Comments of Public Interest Organizations, Docket no. EL25-49-000 (April 13, 2025), Accession No. 20250423-
5243 (“PIO Comments”). 
3 Comments of the Union of Concerned Scientists, Docket no. E;25-49-000 (April 11, 2025), Accession No. 
20250411-5020 (“UCS Comments”).  
4 Show Cause Order ¶ 4, citing PJM Guidance on Co-Located Load (March 22, 2024); Answer of the Indicated PJM 
Transmission Owners to the Order Instituting the Proceeding Under Section 206 of the Federal Power Act and 
Consolidating with Other Proceedings, Docket no. EL25-49-000 (April 23, 2025), Accession No. 20250324-5298 at 
9; Response of Public Service Electric and Gas Company to Show Cause Order issued on 02/20/2025 under EL25-
49, et al., Docket no. EL25-49-000 (March 24, 2025), Accession No. 20250324-5299 at 1. 
5 Answer of PJM Interconnection, LLC, Docket No. EL25-49-000 at 45 (March 24, 2025), Accession No. 
20250324-5313 (“PJM Answer”).

5 
 
 
II. FERC HAS JURISDICTION IN THIS MATTER TO REQUIRE REGIONAL 
TRANSMISSION TARIFF PROVISIONS FOR CO-LOCATED LOAD 
The Federal Power Act tasks the Commission with the regulation of the transmission and 
wholesale sale of electricity to protect the public interest and ensure just and reasonable rates. 16 
U.S.C. §§ 824, 824d. The Commission’s jurisdiction extends over all facilities used for the 
transmission or sale of electric energy in interstate commerce; states maintain jurisdiction over 
the regulation of facilities used for the generation of electricity. 16 U.S.C. § 824. The 
Commission is required to issue an order setting just and reasonable rates, rules, and practices 
whenever it determines that existing rates, rules, and practices involving transmission or 
electricity sales under its jurisdiction are unjust, unreasonable, unduly discriminatory or 
preferential. 16 U.S.C. § 824e. As the Commission sets forth in its Show Cause Order, it has 
authority and jurisdiction to “ensure that rates, charges, and classifications for . . . wholesale sale 
and transmission as well as the practices directly affecting such sale and transmission, are just 
and reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory or preferential.”6   
As the Commission describes at Section VI.A. of the Show Cause Order, the issues raised by 
the interconnection of large loads co-located with generation resources (either new or existing), 
also implicate some state jurisdictional questions.7 However, as noted above and described by 
others, because all co-located generation configurations necessarily receive essential services 
from the transmission grid, this makes them subject to FERC’s jurisdiction and consequently all 
rates, practices, and procedures involving such facilities must be just, reasonable, and not unduly 
discriminatory.8 As such, considerations related to the adequacy of PJM’s tariff to properly plan 
 
6 Show Cause Order, ¶ 66 (citing FERC v. Elec. Power Supply Ass’n, 577 U.S. 260, 278 (2016). 
7 Id., ¶ 67-71. 
8 See UCS Comments at 8-14 (citing Indicated PJM Transmission Owners and NERC to demonstrate how all listed 
configurations cannot be isolated); see id. at 17 (“We illustrate how the fully isolated load idea is a fiction…the

6 
 
 
for and allocate costs pertaining to such large co-located loads is clearly within FERC’s 
jurisdiction under section 206 of the Federal Power Act. 16 U.S.C. §824e. Where, as here, the 
evidence demonstrates that the existing tariff provisions are inadequate, unjust, and 
unreasonable, FERC is obligated to issue new rates, practices, and procedures that comply with 
Federal Power Act requirements. 16 U.S.C. §824d. 
Co-located generation and large load configurations create both the need for additional new 
investment in transmission infrastructure and grid system services, and also sometimes include 
the ability to provide ancillary and other services back to the system. Especially in light of the 
anticipated size of individual generating units and the expected share of the data centers as a 
proportion of future load, it is absolutely critical that grid operators appropriately plan for and 
justly allocate the costs of such investments. As discussed further below, in developing just and 
reasonable rates for co-located load arrangements (particularly any “bring your own generation” 
configuration), the Commission must consider both the full costs of transmission services 
necessary to support such resources, as well as any potential benefits offered by all kinds of co-
located firm generation for system reliability and to meet state clean energy requirements. 
As set forth in Order No. 1920, the Commission’s jurisdiction clearly extends over the 
holistic transmission system planning necessary to properly identify, implement, and pay for the 
facilities and services required to support large load growth.9 Along with Orders 888, 890, and 
1000, these Commission directives represent decades of precedent establishing FERC’s authority 
 
loads require transmission and ancillary services because the host generators are unable to operate without the 
grid.”).  
9 Building for the Future Through Elec. Reg’l Transmission Plan. & Cost Allocation, 89 Fed. Reg. 49,280 (June 11, 
2024), 187 FERC ¶ 61,068 (May 13, 2024), (hereinafter “Order No. 1920”) at ¶¶ 253-258, order on reh’g & 
clarification, Order No, 1920-A, 89 Fed. Reg. 97,14 (Dec. 6, 2024), 189 FERC ¶ 61,126 (2024) order on reh’g & 
clarification, Order No, 1920-B, 191 FERC ¶ 61,026 (Apr. 11, 2025).

7 
 
 
to require transmission stakeholders to meet transmission planning practices and procedures 
necessary to ensure just and reasonable rates.10 Supreme Court Justice Thomas, with Justice 
Scalia and Justice Kennedy concurring in part, have weighed in on FERC’s extensive authority 
over transmission, stating that the Federal Power Act “unambiguously grants FERC jurisdiction 
over all interstate transmission and § 824e mandates that FERC remedy undue discrimination 
with respect to all transmission within its jurisdiction …,” and finding that the statute “require[s] 
FERC … to engage in reasoned decisionmaking to determine whether there is undue 
discrimination with respect to transmission associated with retail bundled sales, and if so, what 
remedy is appropriate.”11 
III. PER ORDER NO. 1920, DATA CENTERS MUST BE INTEGRATED INTO 
LONG TERM PLANNING TO ADDRESS IMPLICATIONS OF LARGE 
LOADS ON TRANMISSION SYSTEM 
While the Commission is asked to look at PJM’s tariff of today, as it considers issuance of a 
broader ruling it must ensure that planning to meet transmission needs associated with large 
loads in the immediate term also aligns with the requirements of Order No. 1920, the central aim 
of which is to ensure that transmission planners accurately identify long-term transmission needs 
and implement efficient and cost-effective solutions to meet those needs.   
As the Commission has found, effective long-term transmission planning is critical to 
unblocking interconnection queue delays that currently thwart the ability to expeditiously bring 
 
10 See, e.g., Transmission Access Policy Study Group v. FERC, 225 F.3d 667, 343 U.S. App. D.C. 151 (D.C. Cir. 
2000) ("TAPS"), aff'd sub nom. New York, 535 U.S. 1 (2002) (upholding Order No. 888 in nearly all respects, 
concluding that the Commission had authority under FPA Section 206 to require open access as a generic remedy 
for systemic anti-competitive behavior); South Carolina Pub. Svc. Comm. v. FERC, 762 F.3d 41, 63 (D.C. Cir. 
2014) (Statute supports Commission's assertion of authority over transmission planning matters in the challenged 
orders, notwithstanding petitioners' contention that the orders intrude on the States' authority). 
11 New York v. FERC, 535 U.S. 1, 42 (2002).

8 
 
 
on new load or develop supply.12 Central to Order No. 1920’s reforms is the transparency of 
information regarding future load and supply, without which the ability of transmission planners 
to meaningfully conduct scenario-based planning and choose the best transmission solutions 
become impossible. The Order No. 1920 planning process must incorporate information about 
expected large loads, with or without co-located generation, in order to ensure that regional 
transmission infrastructure is accurately sized and appropriately located. Such information is also 
essential to ensure that the costs of building the transmission system are fairly assessed and 
allocated. Especially in light of estimates regarding the magnitude of potential load growth from 
data centers, cryptocurrency, electrification, and increased manufacturing, if Order No. 1920 
reforms are to succeed, FERC must require these and other large loads be planned as part of that 
process.  
The system is already experiencing bottlenecks due to the need for additional transmission 
buildout. Studies estimate that a three to four-fold increase in transmission is needed to meet the 
demand of the next thirty years.13 Approximately 2,600 gigawatts of generation and storage 
capacity – of which 95 percent are zero-carbon, low or zero air polluting resources – are waiting 
to connect to the grid today and more transmission is necessary to connect many of these and 
other resources that have been waiting in interconnection queues for years.14 The Commission

(Jul. 18, 2024), https://www.catf.us/2024/07/future-fitting-grid-how-accelerate-federal-transmission-permitting/; 
Clean Air Task Force & Niskanen Center, How are we going to build all that clean energy infrastructure? (Aug. 
2021), https://www.niskanencenter.org/wp-
content/uploads/2021/08/CATF_Niskanen_CleanEnergyInfrastructure_Report.pdf.

Improving the Federal Review and Permitting Processes,

8ec431e6ed26/18CF4B86636126A39982FF1854890BB02118CC591EA301C8C1C3D3307E78AE66.02-19-2025-
pavia-testimony.pdf (citing Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory, Queued Up: Characteristics of Power Plants

9 
 
 
and grid stakeholders have already invested years in building consensus for a path forward to 
deal with all of the resources in need of increased transmission and have embodied those 
solutions in Order Nos. 1920 and 2023.15 Improved regional and interregional transmission will 
alleviate current grid congestion, provide lower-priced energy, and reduce incentives for large 
loads to try and avoid the long delays associated with the planning and interconnection 
processes.16 But if the Commission were to bless the ability of large loads capable of buying 
resources currently relied upon by the entire grid to essentially exempt themselves from these 
processes, those reforms will fail. 
Per Order No. 1920, transmission planners must integrate data centers and co-located 
generation into their long-term planning for upgrading transmission. As stated above, see Section 
I, data centers with co-located generation are not wholly isolated from the grid in the first place 
and thus must not be permitted to be treated as such. The load growth from data centers is 
unprecedented,17 but must be treated as a long-term issue–their usage is but one driver of 
exponential load growth and must be planned for accordingly. While it may appear faster for 
data centers to “skip” the interconnection process and pursue behind-the-meter connections to 
load without connection to the transmission system, evidence in this docket has shown such an 
arrangement to be physically impossible, presenting major risks in reliability and costs to the

Transmission Needs Study (October 2023) 20, 74-79, at: https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/2023-
12/National%20Transmission%20Needs%20Study%20-%20Final_2023.12.1.pdf (hereinafter “National 
Transmission Needs Study”). 
15 Improvements to Generator Interconnection Procedures and Agreements, 184 FERC ¶ 61,054 (2023) (“Order No. 
2023”). 
16 Id. at 32-34.  
17 See Arman Shehabi et al., 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report (Dec. 2024), available at 
https://www.energy.gov/articles/doe-releases-new-report-evaluating-increase-electricity-demand-data-centers 
(showing domestic energy usage from data centers is expected to double or triple by 2028).

10 
 
 
entire grid system.18 Many loads urgently need to be connected to the grid,19 and data centers are 
but one kind of such demand. There is little reason and considerable risk in establishing tariff 
terms that allow data centers and co-located generation to effectively do an end run around the 
much needed and required long-term transmission planning process designated by Order No. 
1920 or the interconnection queue reforms put into place by Order 2023. 
IV. FERC MUST ENSURE COSTS ASSOCIATED WITH CO-LOCATED LARGE 
LOADS ARE FAIRLY ALLOCATED 
Allocating the transmission system costs of co-located loads and generation in a just, 
reasonable, and not unduly discriminatory manner requires a thorough and transparent evaluation 
of the costs and benefits associated with large co-located loads. The need for FERC to act 
expeditiously to establish straightforward rules applicable across the regions is necessary to get 
in front of a rapidly growing industry whose attendant load, costs, and operations could upend 
grid operations if not the Commission does not act. There is already considerable pressure on 
regional and interstate grid operators due to large loads seeking interconnection, with or without 
co-located generation.20 This pressure is exacerbated by interconnection queue delays in PJM 
that have motivated data centers to “skip” the queue via co-location and proposed reshuffling of 
queues.21 There is already clear evidence of such queue skipping occurring, where large loads

19 Nicole Pavia, supra note 14. 
20 National Transmission Needs Study at 87. 
21 See, e.g., Protest of Public Interest Organizations, at 2-4, 6-11, Docket No. ER24-2045 (June 20, 2024), Accession 
No. 20240620-5242 (documenting PJM’s backlogged interconnection queue and significant delays in processing 
interconnection requests); 
Final Brief of Respondent-Intervenors Interconnection Reform Advocates, at 39-44, Advanced Energy United et al. 
v. FERC, Case No. 23-1282, Document No. 211411 (Apr. 16, 2025) (“PJM had, and still has, one of the longest and 
most-backlogged interconnection queues of any region”).

11 
 
 
“shop” multiple queues, making the amount of co-located load pressure on the system seem 
larger than it is.22 
This uncertainty makes planning for such rapid growth both precarious and expensive. As 
PIOs aptly point out, energy costs in the PJM region are skyrocketing, and PJM has already 
issued a call to build $5.9B in new transmission lines needed largely to serve expected growth 
from data centers—incurring immense costs23 that are being borne by PJM’s ratepayers.24 FERC 
has recently approved price ceilings for capacity markets limiting price hikes for consumers,25 
but more needs to be done to ensure that the costs and benefits of transmission infrastructure and 
services associated with the growth of data centers are accurately assessed and justly allocated. 
The evidence of speculation and queue jumping by generators seeking to quickly serve data 
centers via co-location end runs around standard planning and interconnection requirements, 
along with attendant risks to reliability and market manipulation as outlined by PIOs,26 reinforces 
the need to level the planning playing field by requiring co-located generation serving large loads 
to be addressed as part of a holistic grid planning, interconnection, and cost-allocation process 
applicable to all stakeholders connected to the grid. To do otherwise for an economic sector that

conference-regarding-large-loads-co-located-generating-facilities

12 
 
 
is estimated to consume as much as 12 percent of the nation’s electricity as soon as 202827 could 
fatally undermine the critical reforms necessary to develop transmission infrastructure for all 
stakeholders that was achieved as part of Order Nos. 1920 and 2023.   
In order for the cost allocation of improved transmission to be just, reasonable, and not 
unduly discriminatory, FERC must first require clean and transparent accounting of benefits and 
burdens of each large co-located load interconnection for the transmission system and detailed 
accounting of what costs and benefits actually flow to the broader group of ratepayers charged 
with paying them. As other commenters have demonstrated, this is not currently occurring.28 
Transparent and accurate accounting is crucial for ensuring accurate load forecasts that directly 
determine what rates are set.  
Tariffs should also enable potential benefits of co-located load and generator arrangements to 
flow toward the grid, including establishing provisions for co-located facilities to perform 
demand response or other grid services based on the full value of any benefits they may provide 
from either side of the meter. These include but are not limited to avoided investment costs, 
access to lower cost power, or blackstart and other ancillary services, and in certain situations 
where zero- or low-carbon firm generation is co-located, helping states to meet their clean 
energy obligations. Tariff provisions also can and should be written to enable participation by 
any type of resource and establish reasonable penalties for non-performance that reflect the 
operating limitations of the type of resource.29 Co-located generation and storage could increase 
 
27 Arman Shehabi, et al., 2024 United States Data Center Energy Usage Report, 5, LBNL-2001637, Lawrence 
Berkley Nat‘l Lab at: lbnl-2024-united-states-data-center-energy-usage-report.pdf. 
28 See Comments of PIOs, pages 11-14.  
29 Order Denying Complaint, 184 FERC ¶ 61,137 (Aug. 31, 2023), Cmr’s Phillips and Clements concurring, at ¶ 3 
(“Should DIRs become significantly and demonstrably more likely to clear ancillary services when they are 
deliverable, a tariff that fails to allow DIRs to provide those services could be rendered unjust and unreasonable and 
unduly discriminatory or preferential.”)

13 
 
 
the flexibility potential of the net-load of the whole facility (load and generation resources) 
relative to traditional load. As the Nicholas Institute describes in a recently-issued study 
concerning planning for the interconnection of large loads into the U.S. power system, “load 
flexibility can accelerate interconnections, reduce ratepayer costs through higher system 
utilization, and expand the role of demand response, particularly for A.I.-specialized data 
centers,”30 which are of high concern.  
V. PJM’s SUGGESTION THAT THERE IS NEED FOR LESSENED AIR 
POLLUTION STANDARDS FOR CO-LOCATED GENERATION SHOULD 
BE REJECTED 
The Commission can and should prioritize transmission planning and tariff provisions for co-
located configurations that do not rely on additional diesel generator back up supply or the 
lessening of air pollution standards. In response to the Commission’s original request to PJM and 
the Transmission Owners to discuss the benefits of back-up service in co-located load situations, 
PJM suggests an option that would allow more reliance on stationary reciprocating internal 
combustion engines (“RICE”), as back up resources to serve the co-located load when the 
primary co-located generator is not available.31 Additionally, PJM suggests that current 
limitations on the situations and total number of hours when units can be used should be 
loosened “to address resource adequacy concerns in the short term.”32 
CATF disagrees with assertions that current restrictions on the use of diesel RICE must be 
lifted or lessened in order to avoid resource adequacy concerns. As noted above, co-located 
 
30 T. Norris, T. Profeta, D. Patino-Echeverri, A. Cowie-Haskell, Nicholas Institute for Energy, Environment & 
Sustainability, “Rethinking Load Growth Assessing the Potential for Integration of Large Flexible Loads in U.S. 
Power Systems” (February, 2025) at 2, available at: https://nicholasinstitute.duke.edu/publications/rethinking-load-
growth. 
31 PJM Answer at 9, 19, 69-70 & Exh. A (Option 8).   
32 Id. at 70. Notably, a decision to weaken air quality standards is not FERC-jurisdictional.

14 
 
 
generation and loads cannot be fully islanded, and indeed new large loads even where they bring 
their own generation should be considered full transmission system participants. FERC should 
prioritize transmission planning efforts to accommodate even large loads and co-located 
generation interconnections that can alleviate the asserted need for additional onsite diesel 
backup RICE units. 
And, as noted above in the Section IV, co-located loads offer demand response attributes that 
can and should be considered in developing tariff provisions, and in transmission planning 
generally. Where those loads “bring their own generation” resources, those too can provide 
support and ancillary services where interconnected with the transmission system. And where 
co-located generation provides clean firm service, it may also yield a benefit to states in meeting 
their own clean energy standards or portfolio requirements; such benefits also should be 
recognized.33 Those considerations mitigate against the need either for a larger number of back 
up diesel RICE or loosened air quality regulatory requirements on RICE units. 
Importantly, limitations on backup RICE to supply electricity to co-located loads, except in 
emergency situations, are a necessary requirement in order for those RICE units to comply with 
standards established by the Environmental Protection Agency (“EPA”) for the control of 
emissions of hazardous and other air pollutants.34 RICE units emit several toxic air pollutants, 
including formaldehyde and benzene which are known human carcinogens, as well as smog-
 
33 For an explanation of the benefits of clean firm generation, see Clean Air Task Force, Clean Firm Electricity 
Supply and Load Growth (March 26, 2025), https://www.catf.us/events/clean-firm-electricity-supply-load-growth/; 
see also Clean Air Task Force, Tracking clean energy in U.S. states (2025), https://www.catf.us/us/state-
policy/clean-electricity-standards/ (showing state requirements for clean energy). 
34 NESHAP for Hazardous Air Pollutants for Reciprocating Internal Combustion Engines, and New Source 
Performance Standards, 78 Fed. Reg. 6674 (Jan. 30, 2013).

15 
 
 
forming NOx and VOCs, and particulate matter which causes and worsens respiratory ailments.35 
Calls for lessening those requirements are both outside of FERC’s jurisdiction, as the standards 
are completely within EPA’s authority, 42 U.S.C. § 7412, and unnecessary. FERC planning and 
tariff provisions must accommodate co-located loads and generation, assuming all onsite 
generation is compliant with environmental regulations.  
It is CATF’s position that as FERC considers co-located generation and large loads in its 
transmission planning processes, and in developing tariff provisions, there are many transmission 
system benefits offered both by co-located clean firm generating resources, and by the co-located 
large loads, that make the need to add additional RICE or longer run hours for existing RICE 
unnecessary. And CATF disagrees that “accessing this additional [RICE] capability more 
actively” by loosening air quality and public health-beneficial limitations on RICE run time is 
needed to facilitate large load interconnections.36   
VI. CONCLUSION 
CATF applauds FERC’s consideration of these important issues. Increased demand for 
transmission services, driven in part by large loads such as data centers, whether or not co-
located with generation have made careful consideration of how tariff provisions properly can 
support interconnection and transmission access and assure just, reasonable, and non-
discriminatory rates. Co-located large loads and generation cannot be fully isolated from the 
grid, and the costs associated with the additional load, as well as the benefits provided to the 
system and to the states by clean firm co-located generation, must be reflected in rates, practices,

07/documents/ic-engines_ria_reconsider-existing-si-engines_2013-01.pdf.

and procedures that are consistent with transmission access and cost-causation principles 
applicable to all other loads and generators. That analysis must consider the benefits to the grid

additional services the new load or generator will necessarily require. FERC must require large 
loads with co-located generation (such as data centers) to follow the same interconnection
